newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage minister recounts bloody escape.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage minister recounts bloody escape.

text.p: Peru's Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, the key captive of Marxist rebels during Lima's four-month hostage crisis, told on Sunday how he barely escaped alive after being shot twice and having a grenade tossed at him during the bloody finale.

Tudela, in his first interview since the crisis ended, described how the Tupac Amaru guerrillas three times tried to kill him as he crawled and stumbled out of the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence during the April 22 raid by Peruvian commandos.

"One of them tosses the grenade, which must have hit the door and exploded in the air," Tudela told leading daily El Comercio. "If it had exploded on the ground, it would have killed me instantly. I felt a little pinch in the shoulder, which are the shards of grenade."

After this, one rebel shot Tudela in the arm while another caught him in the leg as troops shepherded him over the residence roof and down a staircase to safety. A Peruvian commando died shielding him from the bullets.

Although the 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) members had decided to kill as many hostages as possible, starting with Tudela, only one of the 72 captives died in the battle. All the rebels, and two soldiers were also killed.

Tudela, recovering from his wounds at home after being released from the hospital last week, also confirmed that the MRTA intended to execute one hostage every few hours at the outset of the crisis if the government did not accept its demand for the release of imprisoned comrades.
Conversations with some hostages, who numbered hundreds after the initial Dec. 17 strike on the diplomatic compound, and international attention, persuaded them against this, he added.

In one of the most dramatic moments of the crisis, a deadline came and went for Tudela's execution on the second day of the siege as President Alberto Fujimori decided to brave out MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini.

Tudela, who talked frequently with Cerpa and other MRTA members inside the residence, said the group lacked ideological clarity and its leader became a "megalomaniac" as he saw "the roofs surrounding the residence full of journalists from all around the world; and hears the whole world talking about him when he turns on his radio."
He said this was "one of the saddest aspects of the crisis because this megalomania dragged the other 13 (rebels) to perdition."

The MRTA members paid scant attention to Tudela's attempts to talk them out of their actions. "It was as if I was talking in Greek and them in sanskrit. There was no possibility of understanding," he said.
Cerpa and his second-in-command planned to hold the residence for two months more to maximize the political benefit of the takeover, Tudela added.

The minister also spoke movingly of his personal suffering during 126 days of captivity -- "the fear of death, the uncertainty of each day that passed, going to bed each night without knowing what would happen the next day, if the next day would arrive."
